title: See Where George Custer Was Last Seen Alive (Little Bighorn Battlefield, MT) HMOTD - NewsBreak
text: American History Central's Historical Marker of the Day (HMOTD) is " Custer Last Seen, Little Bighorn Battlefield ." This marker is in Crow Agency, Montana, in Big Horn County, on the Little Bighorn Battlefield Road. Gen. Custer and Lt. Cooke were last seen on this point by Maj. Reno's troops who were fighting in the valley. In 1874, George Custer led an expedition into the Black Hills of the Dakota Territory that confirmed gold in the region, triggering the Black Hills Gold Rush . Within months, illegal trespassing on sacred Native American Indian grounds sparked hostilities between settlers and the Cheyenne and Sioux. The U.S. Army interceded to protect the settlers. In 1876, General Alfred Terry ordered Custer to join forces with General George Crook and Colonel John Gibbon and drive the Sioux and Cheyenne back to their reservations. On June 25, 1876, Custer discovered a Sioux village on the Little Bighorn River and recklessly mounted an independent attack, rather than waiting to act with Crook and Gibbon. Instead of a docile village, Custer soon found that he had charged into a major encampment defended by up to 2,000 Sioux and Cheyenne warriors, led by several notable chiefs, including Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse. The Indians overwhelmed Custer and his men, killing most of them. Along with Custer, his brothers Boston and Thomas, his brother-in-law James Calhoun, and his nephew Henry Reed died at the Battle of the Little Bighorn. Soldiers identified and recovered Custer’s mutilated remains two days after the battle and interred them on the site. One year later, the army moved Custer’s remains to the grounds of the United States Military Academy at West Point, where he received a formal military burial. A Clash Between Cultures The Battle of the Little Bighorn was fought along the ridges, steep bluffs, and ravines of the Little Bighorn River, in south-central Montana on June 25–26, 1876. The combatants were warriors of the Lakota Sioux, Northern Cheyenne, and Arapaho tribes, battling men of the 7th Regiment of the U.S. Cavalry, along with their Crow and Arikara scouts. The Battle of the Little Bighorn symbolizes the clash of two different cultures — the buffalo/horse culture of the northern plains tribes and the highly industrial-based culture of the United States. This battle was not an isolated confrontation, but part of a much larger strategic campaign designed to force the Lakota and Cheyenne to live peacefully on their assigned reservations. The Lakota and Cheyenne fought the U.S. Army from 1865 to 1867. Then, in 1868, several Lakota leaders agreed to sign the Treaty of Fort Laramie . The treaty created a large reservation for the Lakota in the western half of present-day South Dakota, which included the Lakota's sacred Black Hills area. The Federal Government wanted tribes to give up their nomadic life, which brought them into conflict with other Indians, white settlers, and railroads. Agreeing to the treaty meant accepting a more stationary life and relying heavily on the government's promise of supplying food and supplies. Lakota leaders such as Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse rejected the reservation system, as did many roving bands of hunters and warriors. They did not sign the 1868 treaty and became known as "Non-Treaty Indians." Custer's Black Hills Expedition Tension increased in 1874, when Lt. Col. George Armstrong Custer was ordered to explore the Black Hills inside the boundary of the Great Sioux Reservation. Custer was to map the area, locate a suitable site for a future military post, and make note of the natural resources. However, during the expedition, members of his expedition, who were prospectors, discovered deposits of gold. The news spread quickly, and thousands of settlers and prospectors flooded into the Black Hills, violating the Treaty of Fort Laramie. The government negotiated with the Lakota and tried to buy the Black Hills, but the Lakota rejected the offer. In the winter of 1875, a proclamation was issued for all Lakota to report to a reservation by January 31, 1876, or be labeled as "hostiles." The Lakota refused, and the issue became a military matter. Sheridan Sends the Army General Philip Sheridan, commander of the Military Division of Missouri, devised a strategy that required several thousand troops to find and engage the "hostile" Lakota and Cheyenne and force them to the Great Sioux Reservation. The expedition included three columns: Army officials believed that any of these three columns would be able to deal with the 800-1,500 warriors they were likely to encounter. However, there was no plan in place in place for Gibbon, Crook, and Terry to launch a coordinated attack on a specific group of Indians or location. The expedition was slowed by poor communication and the constant movement of the Lakota and Cheyenne, who were often in search of food, water, and grazing areas for their horses. Terry Sends Custer to Make a Flank Attack On June 22, General Terry sent Custer and his cavalry to make a wide flanking march and approach the Indians from the east and south, who were near the Little Bighorn River. Terry hoped this would block the Indians' escape route. Terry planned to approach the camp from the north, with Gibbon, believing these maneuvers would surround the Indians. Custer Finds the Indians Two days later, on June 24, Custer camped 25 miles east of the Indians. He sent his Crow and Arikara scouts to gather intelligence about the Lakota and Cheyenne. The scouts successfully found their camp and reported the location to Custer. He responded by mustering his troops and ordering a night march that crossed to the Little Bighorn River Valley. Early on June 25, the 7th Cavalry Regiment was near the Wolf Mountains, about 12 miles from the Indian encampment along the Little Bighorn River. Custer intended to launch a surprise attack on the camp, but found out the Indians had seen his column. At Wolf Mountain, Custer divided his troops: Custer's Attack Begins Custer sent Benteen southwest to engage any Indians they encountered. When Custer was informed that the Indians in the village were scattering, he and Reno moved forward to attack. However, Custer had not seen the camp and was unaware of how many Indians awaited him. Reno's Attack The camp was just west of the Little Bighorn River. Reno crossed the river about 2 miles south of the village. Initially surprised, the Indians rushed to defend against Reno's attack. The Indians pressed their attack, and Reno ordered a second retreat, this time to the bluffs east of the river. Reno recrossed the Little Bighorn River and regrouped on the high ground east of the camp. Custer's Attack Meanwhile, Custer rode north and encountered Indians, who forced him to fall back to Calhoun Hill. Benteen Joins Reno Benteen did not encounter any Indians and arrived on the high ground just as Reno's survivors were gathering. Benteen had received a message from Custer that said, "Come on. Big Village. Be Quick. Bring Packs. P.S. Bring Packs." After hearing gunfire, they tried to locate Custer and sent some troops north to see if they could find him. These men moved to a high point about 1.5 miles north of where Reno was. From there, they could see the battlefield, which was engulfed in smoke and dust. Custer's Last Stand After forcing Reno to retreat, the Indians engaged Custer and his men, who moved along a ridge north of the camp. They were overwhelmed and forced to withdraw to a small hill. By this time, it is estimated that only 40 men, including Custer, were still alive. Although they held out as long as they could, they were overwhelmed, and every man in Custer's command was killed. It was a brief victory for the Lakota and Cheyenne. The death of Custer and his troops became a rallying point for the United States to increase its efforts to force Indians onto reservation lands. With more troops in the field, Lakota hunting grounds were invaded by powerful Army expeditionary forces determined to conquer the Northern Plains Indians. Most of the declared "hostiles" surrendered within one year of the fight, and the government took the Black Hills without compensation to the Lakota.
